strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in visual robot navigation: learning a robust RGB-only policy that can handle narrow passages, dynamic obstacles, and difficult-to-detect objects under sim-to-real transfer.

The proposed system is practically compelling: four-view 360-degree visual input, continuous velocity prediction, and a 7B VLA backbone running at about 7 Hz on real robot hardware. The setup is more deployment-oriented than many language-guided navigation papers with discrete actions or purely simulated evaluation.

The multi-expert training recipe is sensible and fairly well motivated. Training privileged depth-based RL experts for reaching, squeezing, and avoiding, then distilling them into a unified RGB VLA student via offline and online DAgger-like iterations, is a coherent way to obtain challenging supervision without unsafe real-world collection.

Simulation results show clear gains over iPlanner, ViPlanner, and NavDP across four settings, especially in squeezing and dynamic avoidance, where the surround-view design is plausibly important. The ablations on iterative training, capability-balanced sampling, and mixed versus single-expert training support the main design choices.

The manuscript is generally readable, with a clear pipeline, implementation details for the RL experts and VLA training, and real-world demonstrations that qualitatively suggest meaningful sim-to-real robustness.
weaknesses: No contribution type is explicitly declared, so I assess it as Algorithms/General. Under that framing, the novelty is moderate rather than strong: the method combines known ingredients, including multi-view perception, VLA fine-tuning, privileged RL expert distillation, and DAgger-style data aggregation. The capability-balanced sampling rule is useful but relatively simple.

The real-world evaluation is mostly qualitative. The paper claims extensive real-world experiments and robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, but provides no success rates, number of trials, collision counts, path lengths, failure cases, or comparisons to baselines on the physical robot. This is a major evidence gap for a deployment-oriented navigation paper.

The simulation comparisons may not fully isolate the proposed algorithmic contributions. Baselines such as NavDP/iPlanner/ViPlanner appear disadvantaged by their original front-view or different sensing/control assumptions, while the proposed method uses four cameras and omnidirectional continuous velocity. There is no strong same-sensor baseline or ablation separating the effect of 360-degree input from the VLA/multi-expert training strategy.

Several important ablations are missing or only partially shown: front-only versus four-view VLA, VLA backbone versus smaller non-language policy with the same data, continuous velocity versus discretized actions, QA co-training versus no QA, and offline-only versus online DAgger under matched data budgets.

Some claims are stronger than the presented numbers support. For example, the paper states that the student outperforms the RL teachers, but the evidence is mixed and mostly based on selected metrics/figures; Table II shows specialized RL teachers remain stronger for some individual capabilities than certain students, and the exact RL teacher performance used for comparison is not always transparent.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The reward components are described only at a high level, many environment-generation details are underspecified, real-world calibration/control details are sparse, and there is no clear commitment to release code, trained models, datasets, or simulation assets. Statistical variation across seeds or confidence intervals is also absent.

The paper has presentation issues that make assessment harder: some table formatting is hard to parse, figure text is crowded, real-world scenes are inconsistently named, and the writing occasionally overstates conclusions relative to the evidence. A limitations and failure-mode discussion is largely missing.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: robust RGB-only local navigation in cluttered, narrow, and dynamic environments. The 360-degree multi-camera setup and continuous velocity output are well motivated for real robot deployment.

The overall training recipe is coherent: train capability-specific depth-privileged RL experts, distill them into a multi-view VLA student, and refine with an online DAgger-style aggregation loop. This is a plausible systems contribution even if the algorithmic novelty is limited.

The manuscript includes several useful ablations, especially comparing single-expert versus mixed-expert training and balanced versus unbalanced data aggregation. These results support the intuition that multi-capability data is beneficial.
The paper reports both simulation experiments and real-world demonstrations on a Unitree GO2 with four cameras, including narrow passages, thin obstacles, and dynamic obstacles.
weaknesses: The evidence is not strong enough for the paper's broad claims of robust sim-to-real transfer and strong navigation capability. The real-world evaluation is almost entirely qualitative; no success rates, trial counts, failure cases, baselines, or statistical summaries are provided for the physical robot experiments.

The simulation comparisons are not well controlled. The main baselines appear to use single/front-view sensing or different perception/action assumptions, while the proposed method uses four cameras and continuous omnidirectional velocity. Without sensor- and action-matched baselines, it is unclear whether the gains come from the VLA/multi-expert learning method or simply from more favorable sensing and control.

The reported robustness is questionable: even the proposed method has substantial collision rates in simulation, e.g. 20% in reaching and 32% in avoiding, and only 47% success in the mixed scene. These numbers are not consistent with the strongest claims of robust deployment.

The novelty is modest. Multi-view observation, privileged-expert distillation, DAgger-style online imitation, VLA fine-tuning, and weighted data balancing are all fairly standard components. The paper does not clearly isolate a new technical idea beyond combining these ingredients.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing or underspecified: full reward definitions, environment generation details, exact prompts, VQA subset construction, training schedules, online data collection criteria, camera calibration/undistortion, goal localization in the real robot, and whether code/data will be released.

The ablations are incomplete. There is no direct comparison to a non-VLA multi-view policy with the same data, a VLA without QA co-training, a model without history, two-camera/four-camera variants under matched training, or a depth/RGB privileged oracle under the same evaluation. These omissions make it difficult to attribute performance to the claimed design choices.

Some claims appear overstated or internally imprecise. For example, the paper says the student outperforms RL experts, but Table II shows the mixed VLA does not outperform the squeezing RL expert on squeezing success rate. The text also relies on WTT in some places and success rate in others without a careful discussion of tradeoffs.

The experimental protocol is narrow: all main quantitative evaluations are in custom IsaacLab scenes designed by the authors, with only 100 episodes per scene and no confidence intervals or significance analysis. The mixed scene is said to have reduced squeezing difficulty, which further weakens the generalization claim.

The paper is written clearly enough to follow, but it has several presentation issues: overloaded figures, hard-to-read plots/tables, vague claims such as 'extensive real-world experiments,' and limited discussion of limitations or safety failure modes despite high collision rates.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic paper. Under that lens, the main contribution is compelling: MM-Nav combines multi-view RGB perception, a VLA policy, and multi-expert RL distillation into a practical visual navigation system for challenging robot settings.

The problem is important and timely. Robust visual-only navigation with 360-degree perception, continuous velocity control, and sim-to-real transfer is highly relevant to embodied vision and robotics, and the focus on squeezing, reaching, and dynamic obstacle avoidance targets meaningful real-world failure modes.

The system design is technically sensible. The use of privileged depth-based RL experts in simulation, followed by RGB-only VLA student training and DAgger-style online aggregation, is a coherent way to exploit simulation while deploying with cheaper visual sensing.

The experimental results are strong in simulation. Across 100 episodes per scene, MM-Nav substantially outperforms iPlanner, ViPlanner, and NavDP on success rate in squeezing, avoiding, and mixed settings, with especially large gains in narrow-gap and dynamic-obstacle scenarios.

The ablations support the central claims. The paper studies online training iterations, capability-balanced data aggregation, and single-expert versus mixed-expert training, showing that multi-expert learning and balancing improve cross-capability performance rather than merely adding capacity.

The real-world demonstrations are valuable. The paper reports deployment on a Unitree GO2 with four fisheye cameras and shows qualitative transfer to thin obstacles, narrow passages, clutter, transparent materials, and dynamic intrusions, which strengthens the practical case for the method.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. Many ingredients are established or natural extensions of prior work: multi-view perception, VLA finetuning, privileged expert distillation, DAgger-style aggregation, and weighted sampling. The contribution is more convincing as an integrated system than as a fundamentally new method.

The real-world evaluation is mostly qualitative. Given the strong claims about robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, the paper would be substantially stronger with real-world success/collision rates, trial counts, comparisons to baselines or the robot's native navigation stack, and failure cases.

The baseline comparison is somewhat uneven. The main simulated baselines appear to use more limited sensing or different action/policy assumptions, especially single/front-view perception, while MM-Nav uses four-view 360-degree RGB. This supports the usefulness of surround perception but makes it harder to isolate the contribution of the VLA and multi-expert training.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact scene generation parameters, reward definitions beyond high-level terms, VQA subset selection, prompt formatting, training schedules, online data collection protocol, and baseline adaptation choices are not specified enough for straightforward replication.

The evaluation would benefit from more controlled ablations, such as front-view versus four-view MM-Nav, VLA versus a smaller non-LLM student under the same data, no-VQA cotuning, no-history variants, and comparisons to a multi-view version of NavDP or other stronger adapted baselines.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. For example, the paper states that MM-Nav proves synergistic multi-capability learning and robust sim-to-real transfer, but the mechanism is only partially isolated and the real-world evidence lacks quantitative support. The conclusion should be more measured.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: visual-only point-goal navigation in cluttered, dynamic, and narrow real-world settings. The proposed combination of 360-degree RGB observations, continuous velocity prediction, specialized RL teachers, and VQA co-training is well motivated for sim-to-real navigation.

The experimental results are promising. MM-Nav substantially outperforms prior methods on the InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, including RGB-D/depth baselines, and also performs best on the authors' custom IsaacLab reaching/squeezing/avoiding/mixed environments.

The paper includes useful ablations for VQA co-training, multi-view versus single-view input, iterative teacher-student refinement, capability-balanced aggregation, and expert-combination strategy. These ablations support several of the main design choices rather than only reporting a final model.

The system aspect is compelling: a 7B VLA model running at about 7 Hz with four-camera surround view and demonstrated on a Unitree GO2 suggests practical relevance beyond offline benchmark evaluation.
The appendix gives additional details on the RL expert environments, reward formulation, PPO setup, and training curves, which helps clarify the expert-data generation process.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The main ingredients, including VLA navigation, privileged expert distillation, DAgger-style aggregation, multi-view perception, and VQA co-training, are largely extensions or combinations of recent ideas. The capability-balanced sampling rule is sensible but technically simple, so the contribution rests heavily on empirical validation.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. The strongest reported model uses four-camera 360-degree input and offboard RTX 5090 inference, while many baselines use different sensors, fields of view, action spaces, platforms, and original configurations. The single-view variant helps, but the main headline numbers still benefit from a substantially richer observation setup.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but limited in scientific strength. Only four representative scenarios are discussed, the VQA ablation uses 20 trials per scenario, and the paper does not provide enough detail on route lengths, start/goal distributions, failure modes, statistical variation, or whether scenarios were selected post hoc. This weakens claims of robust real-world generalization.

The custom IsaacLab benchmark is useful but not independently validated, and all capability-specific test environments are close to the training story. The mixed scene is said to be out of distribution, but the degree of novelty is unclear. Results would be stronger with more public benchmarks or held-out environment generators.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the paper says the student outperforms the RL teachers and demonstrates synergistic capability integration, but this is mostly shown in the authors' setup and with teachers that have a depth-based policy but narrow specialization. It remains unclear how much gain comes from model scale, multi-view input, VQA data, or aggregation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript gives many hyperparameters, but does not clearly state whether code, trained models, expert trajectories, VQA subset construction, simulator assets, and real-world evaluation protocols will be released. Training and deployment also require substantial compute and hardware.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and societal-impact discussion. Important issues such as safety in crowded public spaces, failure recovery, latency/network dependence, robustness to camera calibration errors, moving people, and deployment responsibility are not adequately addressed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important visual navigation problem: RGB-only, 360-degree, continuous-velocity point-goal navigation in cluttered and dynamic settings. The target capability set of reaching, squeezing, and obstacle avoidance is relevant and practically meaningful.

The proposed system is reasonably complete from a systems perspective, combining privileged RL teachers, VLA distillation, iterative data aggregation, multi-view observation encoding, and real-robot deployment. The 7 Hz reported inference rate for a 7B model is a useful engineering result.

The paper includes several ablations: VQA co-training, single-view vs. multi-view input, iterative refinement, capability-balanced aggregation, and single-expert vs. mixed-expert training. These help support some of the design choices.

The reported quantitative gains are large on the InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark and on the authors' IsaacLab benchmark, and the real-world examples cover visually challenging cases such as thin wires, cluttered corridors, pedestrians, and night outdoor navigation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for the strength of the claims. The main public benchmark comparison is potentially confounded: the proposed method uses multi-view RGB and continuous omnidirectional control, while many baselines are front-view or RGB-D/depth systems with different sensing/control assumptions. The paper reports a single-view variant, but does not provide equally adapted multi-view or continuous-control versions of strong baselines.

The custom IsaacLab benchmark appears tailored to the three training capabilities and to the proposed 360-degree perception setup. Baselines perform extremely poorly in squeezing and mixed scenes, but it is unclear whether they were fairly adapted, tuned, or given comparable sensing. This makes the large margins hard to interpret.

The real-world evidence is mostly qualitative. The VQA ablation has 20 trials per scenario, but the paper gives limited protocol detail, no statistical uncertainty, no failure taxonomy, no safety intervention reporting, and no comparison to real-world baselines. The claims of strong zero-shot sim-to-real transfer therefore remain under-supported.

The methodological novelty is incremental. Multi-expert RL distillation, DAgger-style aggregation, VLA fine-tuning, VQA co-training for sim-to-real, and multi-view token pooling are plausible combinations, but the paper does not clearly establish a fundamentally new algorithmic idea beyond system integration.

Several important implementation and reproducibility details are vague or inconsistent. The abstract claims 1.5M expert demonstrations, while the method describes 500k initial steps plus 200k per iteration and 100k/40k VQA data; it is unclear whether these are episodes, steps, or total samples. The VQA subset, data collection protocol, benchmark release status, and training/evaluation code availability are not clearly specified.

The claim that the VLA student outperforms the RL teachers is not fully convincing. The RL teachers are specialized, use depth, and are evaluated under different distributional conditions; the paper does not isolate whether the gains come from multi-capability fusion, model scale/pretraining, VQA co-training, or benchmark mismatch.

Presentation quality is uneven. Some formulas and extracted text appear garbled, terminology such as 'demonstrations' versus 'steps' is imprecise, and some discussion overstates conclusions relative to the evidence. A limitations and societal/safety discussion is also largely missing despite deployment on a real robot in human environments.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and practically relevant Algorithms/General contribution for visual robot navigation: a 7B multi-view VLA policy that maps 360-degree RGB observations and point-goal prompts to continuous omnidirectional velocity commands.

The core recipe is compelling: specialized privileged RL experts for reaching, squeezing, and dynamic avoidance are distilled into a unified student, then refined with a DAgger-like online teacher-student loop and capability-balanced sampling. This is a reasonable and original integration of RL expertise, VLA pretraining, and multi-view control.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally strong. MM-Nav substantially improves over prior methods on the InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, including an 88.1% average success rate for the multi-view variant, and it performs well in custom reaching/squeezing/avoiding/mixed IsaacLab environments.

The ablation studies are useful: the paper isolates the effects of VQA co-training, multi-view perception, iterative refinement, capability-balanced aggregation, and expert combination. These support the main design choices rather than merely reporting a single final number.

The real-world demonstrations, while not exhaustive, are valuable. The paper evaluates challenging cases such as thin wires, cluttered corridors with glass, pedestrian avoidance, and nighttime outdoor navigation, showing plausible sim-to-real transfer from RGB-only perception.

The method is described with enough architectural and training detail to understand the system, including tokenization strategy, action head, PPO expert setup, reward coefficients, data sizes, iteration budgets, and deployment hardware.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation is still relatively limited for the strength of the deployment claims. It uses selected representative scenarios and 20 trials per ablation setting, but does not provide broader statistics across many environments, failure modes, or comparisons to real-robot baselines under identical hardware.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. The proposed full model uses four-view RGB and continuous omnidirectional control, while several baselines are single-view or have different sensing/control assumptions. The single-view ablation helps, but the headline gains partly reflect system-level advantages beyond the proposed learning strategy.

The custom IsaacLab benchmark is useful but author-designed, and the baselines appear to be evaluated mostly under their original configurations. More detail on baseline adaptation, tuning, and whether each method receives comparable observations would make the comparison more convincing.

The sim-to-real benefit of VQA co-training is plausible and supported by ablations, but the mechanism remains somewhat indirect. The VQA data source, filtering, exact task format, and possible overlap or domain bias are not described in enough depth to fully assess reproducibility and attribution.

The system requires a large 7B model running on a remote RTX 5090 server at about 7 Hz. This is impressive for the model size, but the paper could better discuss latency, communication robustness, onboard feasibility, and safety implications when commands are generated offboard.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations section. Important issues such as failure cases, sensitivity to camera calibration/FOV, transparent or reflective surfaces, dynamic human safety, and cross-embodiment transfer are only lightly discussed or deferred to future work.

There are presentation issues, including occasional grammar problems, awkward notation, and some claims that are stated more strongly than the evidence warrants, such as broad claims of robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. These do not undermine the main contribution but do affect clarity and polish.
